body.text: A **transfer price** is the price one subsidiary of a TNC charges another subsidiary of the same TNC for goods, services, loans or the use of a brand. Because both sides belong to the same firm, it can set the price wherever it likes. Setting it so that profit is recorded in a low-tax country is **transfer pricing** used for tax avoidance.

A TNC mines copper in Country H, where profit is taxed at 30%, at a cost of $60m, and sells it through its own trading arm in Country L, taxed at 5%, which sells it on for $100m. If the trading arm pays the market price, the whole profit is in H and tax is $12m. If the TNC sets a transfer price of $65m, most of the profit appears in L and total tax falls to $3.25m; Country H loses $10.5m.

**The regulation of transfer pricing** rests on the **arm's-length principle**: the price between two parts of a TNC must be the price two independent firms would agree. Tax authorities can compare transfer prices with world market prices, demand documentation, agree prices in advance with a firm, and reassess tax where the price was not at arm's length. For commodities with a quoted world price, this is easier than for brands and patents, which have no market price.

realExample.text: Zambia's tax authority has challenged mining companies over copper sold to related trading companies abroad at prices below those on world markets, and has raised tax assessments as a result.

sections.misconception: Students treat any trade between subsidiaries as tax avoidance. Firms must trade internally; the problem is a transfer price set away from the market price to move profit.
sections.examMatters: Work a transfer-pricing example in figures when the data allow: profit and tax in each country at the market price and at the transfer price. It shows exactly what the regulation protects.

recall.prompt: Sort each price charged between two parts of the same TNC by how a tax authority applying the arm's-length principle would treat it:

groups.name: Accepted: at arm's length
items: A mine invoices its sister sales company for copper at the day's quoted metal price
A loan between two subsidiaries at the interest rate a bank would charge
Engine parts sold to a sister plant at the price charged to outside buyers
groups.why: Each price is what two independent firms would agree, so profit is recorded where the work is done.

groups.name: Challenged: not at arm's length
items: Ore sold to its own trading arm at half the world price
A management fee charged to the mine at three times what an outside consultant charges
A loan from a low-tax subsidiary at triple the market interest rate
groups.why: Each price is set away from the market price, which can shift profit to where tax is low.

sections.title: Limits to Government Ability to Control TNCs
sections.keyIdea: TNCs are mobile, powerful and well advised, so one government acting alone can do only so much: they can move, lobby or out-resource a tax authority.

body.text: The specification also asks for the **limits to government ability to control TNCs**. The main ones:

items: **Mobility** — a TNC can move production, profits or headquarters to another country. A government that taxes or regulates harshly may lose the investment and jobs altogether, so governments compete to attract TNCs rather than control them.
**Information** — the TNC knows its own costs and internal prices; the tax authority must reconstruct them. Brands, patents and services have no market price to check against.
**Resources** — the largest TNCs have revenues larger than the GDP of many countries, and can employ more accountants and lawyers than a developing country's entire tax authority.
**Jurisdiction** — a government can tax and regulate only within its own borders. Without international agreement, profit moved abroad is out of reach.
**Political influence** — TNCs lobby governments and can threaten to withdraw.

body.text: International cooperation, such as the OECD minimum tax and information sharing between tax authorities, eases some of these limits. It depends on enough countries joining, and on low-tax countries accepting it.

realExample.text: Several African tax authorities have sought outside support to audit multinational mining companies, whose accounts and internal pricing are more complex than their own staff can check alone.

sections.misconception: Students write that governments cannot control TNCs at all. They can and do, through tax rules, regulation and agreements; the limits are about how far one country can go alone.
sections.examMatters: An Evaluate (20 marks, Appendix 6) on controlling TNCs needs the measures and their limits weighed, not listed. The strongest judgement explains why international cooperation changes the answer.

recall.prompt: Sort each point by which limit on controlling TNCs it shows: mobility or information:

groups.name: Mobility
items: A chip maker says it will build its next plant elsewhere if taxes rise
A bank shifts its regional headquarters after new rules are announced
A clothing firm moves its orders to factories in a neighbouring country
groups.why: Each shows the firm can move activity away from a government that acts against it.

groups.name: Information
items: The tax office cannot tell what a licence to use a logo is really worth
Auditors must rely on the firm's own figures for its internal costs
No world price exists for software sold between two branches
groups.why: Each shows the government lacks the facts it needs to check what the firm reports.

sections.title: The Impact of Policy Changes on Local, National and Global Economies
sections.keyIdea: One policy change works at three levels: on particular towns and regions, on the national economy, and, for large economies, on the rest of the world.

body.text: The specification asks for **the impact of policy changes** on local economies, national economies and the global economy. The same decision can look very different at each level.

items: **Local economies** — a policy can hit particular regions hardest. Removing a fuel subsidy raises transport costs most in rural areas far from markets; closing a state-owned plant devastates the town it employs; a new port transforms the coast it serves.
**National economies** — the effect on aggregate demand, output, inflation, the fiscal deficit and the balance of payments.

**The global economy** — policies in large economies spill across borders. When the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates, capital flows out of emerging economies, their currencies fall and their borrowing costs rise. A large economy's stimulus or recession changes its trading partners' exports.

body.text: The levels can pull in opposite directions: a policy that is good for the national budget may be painful for particular regions, and one that suits a large economy may export problems to smaller ones.

realExample.text: When Nigeria removed its petrol subsidy, fares and food prices rose sharply in cities and rural areas alike, while the national budget saved money that had gone on the subsidy.

sections.misconception: Students assess a policy only at national level. An answer that also says which regions lose, and how other countries are affected, shows the fuller judgement the specification asks for.
sections.examMatters: When a question says "the impact of policy changes", organise your answer by the three levels in the specification: local, national and global. Each is a place for a separate chain of reasoning.

recall.prompt: Sort each effect of a policy change by the level of economy it describes: local, national or global:

groups.name: Local
items: A fishing town loses its cannery when a state subsidy ends
Farm incomes in one province rise after a new highway opens
groups.why: Each falls on a particular town or region.

groups.name: National
items: The country's inflation rate climbs by two points
The fiscal deficit narrows by 1% of GDP
groups.why: Each is a change in a whole-economy measure.

groups.name: Global
items: Currencies across Asia weaken after US rates rise
Exporters in other countries win more orders after a large economy's stimulus
groups.why: Each crosses borders to affect other economies.

sections.title: Problems for Policymakers: Inaccurate Information, Risks and Uncertainties
sections.keyIdea: Policymakers act on data that are late and often revised, and on predictions of effects that are uncertain, so well-intended policy can be wrongly sized or wrongly timed.

body.text: The specification names three **problems facing policymakers when applying policies**. The first two are about knowledge.

**Inaccurate information.** Economic data arrive late and are revised. The first estimate of GDP growth may be changed months later; unemployment and inflation are measured by surveys with errors; the informal economy is largely missing from official figures. A central bank may raise rates to cool an economy that the later, corrected data show was already slowing.
**Risks and uncertainties.** Even with good data, the effects of a policy are uncertain:

items: **Time lags** — a change in interest rates can take a year or more to affect inflation, so policy must act on forecasts.
**Uncertain size of effects** — how much households spend from a tax cut depends on their confidence, which nobody can measure in advance.
**Expectations** — if people expect a tax cut to be reversed, they may save it.
**Unintended consequences** — a price cap can cause shortages; a tax rise can drive activity into the informal sector.

realExample.text: When Nigeria revised the way it measures GDP to include newer industries such as telecoms and film, the size of its economy was raised by almost 90% overnight, changing every ratio based on it.

sections.misconception: Students blame poor policy on bad intentions or weak governments. Even well-run central banks and treasuries act on data that turn out to be wrong and on effects they cannot measure in advance.
sections.examMatters: In a 20-mark evaluation, the problems facing policymakers are the evaluation: say which data were uncertain, how long the lag might be, and what could make the effect larger or smaller than intended.

recall.prompt: Sort each problem by the specification's category: inaccurate information or risks and uncertainties:

groups.name: Inaccurate information
items: Last quarter's growth figure is revised from 3% to 1%
Half of all workers are in unregistered jobs the surveys miss
Price data for rural areas are collected only once a year
groups.why: Each is about the figures policymakers rely on being wrong, late or incomplete.

groups.name: Risks and uncertainties
items: Nobody knows whether households will spend or save a tax rebate
A rate rise may not reach inflation for eighteen months
A price cap on rice may cause farmers to grow less of it
groups.why: Each is about how a policy will work, even when the data are sound.

sections.title: Problems for Policymakers: Inability to Control External Shocks
sections.keyIdea: A government cannot control world oil prices, foreign recessions, pandemics or wars, so a policy can be blown off course by events it had no way to prevent.

body.text: The third problem is the **inability to control external shocks**. Policy is planned on assumptions about the world economy, and those assumptions can be overturned: world commodity prices swing, trading partners fall into recession, pandemics, wars and natural disasters strike, and investors withdraw capital from whole regions at once.

A government can prepare, but it cannot prevent. It can build foreign-currency reserves, keep its debt low enough to borrow in a crisis, diversify its exports, and use automatic stabilisers. When the shock comes, though, it must respond to events it did not choose, and a policy designed for one situation, such as a plan to cut the deficit, may have to be abandoned.

Small, open economies are the most exposed. An economy where exports are a large share of GDP, which imports most of its fuel and food, or which relies on one commodity or on tourism, feels a shock abroad as a large shock at home.

realExample.text: When a war in Europe sent world wheat and fuel prices soaring, importers such as Egypt, Pakistan and Sri Lanka saw inflation jump and their foreign-currency reserves drain, whatever their own policies had been.

sections.misconception: Students treat a policy that failed after an external shock as a bad policy. It may have been sound on the information available; the shock is a reason for failure the government could not control.
sections.examMatters: When an extract mentions events abroad, use them as evaluation: the policy's success depended on conditions the government could not control, and name one way it could have prepared.

recall.prompt: Name what each government did to prepare for shocks it could not control:
template: It kept export earnings in the central bank as ___ to sell in a crisis.
It kept its borrowing low so that it could run a larger ___ when a recession struck.
It developed tourism and manufacturing so it no longer relied on one ___.
hints: assets a central bank can sell to support its currency
the gap between spending and revenue in a year
a single raw material sold abroad

takeaway: TNC tax avoidance is fought with minimum taxes and reporting rules.
Transfer prices must match an arm's-length market price.
Bad data, uncertain effects and shocks limit every policy.

notes.title: Public Expenditure
notes.keyIdea: The three kinds of public expenditure, and the three reasons the specification gives for its changing size and pattern across countries.

items.text: Capital expenditure — public spending on assets that last: roads, schools, hospitals, ports.
Current expenditure — public spending on goods and services used up within the year: salaries, medicines, running costs.
Transfer payments — payments to individuals with no good or service received in return: pensions, benefits, grants.
Solmara: capital $24bn + current $84bn + transfers $52bn = $160bn, 40% of GDP.
Changing incomes: richer economies demand more health and education, much of it publicly provided.
Changing age distributions: ageing raises pensions and health; a young population needs schools. Changing expectations: citizens come to expect more and better services.

takeaway: Transfers are public expenditure but not spending on output.
Incomes, age distributions and expectations change the pattern.
Ageing shifts spending rather than raising all of it.

notes.title: Public Spending as a Share of GDP
notes.keyIdea: Why the share of GDP spent by the state matters: for productivity and growth, for crowding out, and for the levels of taxation needed to pay for it.

items.text: Crowding out — a fall in private spending caused by a rise in public spending, chiefly through higher interest rates on borrowing.
Public expenditure as a proportion of GDP — public spending divided by GDP, the usual measure of the size of the state.
Borrow $20bn → rates 4% → 5% → investment −$8bn → net addition $12bn.
Infrastructure, education and health raise output per worker; subsidies to failing firms rarely do.
A larger state needs a larger tax share: see the effects of tax changes in 2c.

takeaway: What spending buys matters more than its share of GDP.
Crowding out is largest near full capacity with high rates.
Borrowing postpones taxation; it does not replace it.

notes.title: Taxes: Types, Incentives and Revenue
notes.keyIdea: Direct and indirect taxes, the three tax structures, and how changes in tax rates affect incentives to work, tax revenue and the distribution of income.

items.text: Direct tax — on income or wealth (income tax, corporation tax). Indirect tax — on spending (VAT or GST, excise duties).
Progressive / proportional / regressive — the share of income taken rises / stays the same / falls as income rises.
Laffer curve — tax revenue against the tax rate: rising to a peak, then falling as the tax base shrinks.
Solmara's income tax: average rates 5%, 19%, 24.5% at incomes of $10,000, $50,000, $100,000.
A 10% sales tax takes 9%, 6% and 4% of the same incomes: regressive.
Marginal rate 30% → 40%: an extra $1,000 earns $600 instead of $700.

takeaway: Judge a tax structure by the share of income, not the dollars.
Nobody knows where the Laffer peak lies.
Progressive taxes narrow the income gap; sales taxes widen it.

notes.title: Tax Changes and the Macroeconomy
notes.meta: 4.3.5 · 2c (output and employment, price level, trade balance, FDI)
notes.keyIdea: How changes in direct and indirect tax rates affect real output and employment, the price level, the trade balance and flows of foreign direct investment.

items.text: Marginal propensity to import — the share of an extra dollar of income spent on imports.
FDI — investment by a firm in productive assets it controls in another country.
Income tax cut → disposable income up → consumption up → AD right → output and jobs up (with spare capacity).
Indirect tax rise → costs up → SRAS left → price level up, output down.
Tax cut $10bn × MPM 0.3 = imports up $3bn. Corporation tax 25% → 15%: return 15% → 17%.

takeaway: Spare capacity decides whether a tax cut raises output or prices.
Draw an indirect tax rise as an SRAS shift, not an AD shift.
Tax is one factor in FDI location among many.

notes.title: Fiscal Deficits and the National Debt
notes.keyIdea: Deficits and surpluses, deficits and the debt, automatic and discretionary policy, structural and cyclical deficits, what drives them and why their size matters.

items.text: Fiscal deficit / surplus — public spending above / below revenue in one year.
National debt — the stock of government borrowing still owed: past deficits minus surpluses.
Automatic stabilisers — tax and benefit changes that happen without a decision. Discretionary policy — deliberate changes.
Cyclical deficit — the part caused by the cycle. Structural deficit — the part left at full capacity.
Debt $240bn + deficit $16bn = $256bn; a surplus of $6bn → $250bn.
Recession: tax −$8bn, benefits +$4bn → deficit $28bn = structural $16bn + cyclical $12bn.
Debt interest $240bn × 5% = $12bn, 8.3% of revenue.

takeaway: Only a surplus reduces the debt in dollars.
Cyclical deficits fade with recovery; structural ones need a decision.
Borrowing for lasting assets is fairer to future taxpayers.

notes.title: Macroeconomic Policies in Use
notes.keyIdea: How the five policy tools are used to reduce deficits and debt, control inflation, respond to external shocks and reduce poverty and inequality, and the response to the 2008 crisis.

items.text: Exchange-rate policy — influencing the currency's value through interest rates or reserves.
Direct controls — rules that set prices, wages, trade or capital flows directly.
External shock — an event outside the economy that changes it: a global recession, a price jump, a pandemic.
Deficits: tax up / spending down, helped by low rates and growth; risk: output falls and revenue with it.
Inflation: higher rates, fiscal tightening, a stronger currency, controls; match the tool to the cause.
Fiscal and monetary instruments are topic 2.3.6; exchange rate systems are 4.3.3; poverty measures are 4.3.4.

takeaway: Name the tool and its channel before its effect.
A supply shock cannot be fixed by demand stimulus alone.
The response to the 2008 crisis worked but left national debts much higher.

notes.title: TNCs and the Limits of Policy
notes.keyIdea: Measures to control TNCs and their limits, the impact of policy at local, national and global level, and the problems policymakers face.

items.text: Tax avoidance — legally arranging affairs to pay less tax. Tax evasion — illegal non-payment.
Transfer price — the price one part of a TNC charges another; regulated by the arm's-length principle.
Copper at cost $60m, sold at $100m: tax $12m at arm's length, $3.25m at a transfer price of $65m.
Limits: mobility, information, resources, jurisdiction, lobbying.
Problems: inaccurate information, risks and uncertainties, inability to control external shocks.

takeaway: International agreement is what makes TNC controls bite.
Judge a policy at local, national and global level.
Policy acts on revised data and uncertain effects.

quiz.question: Which of these is a transfer payment?
options: the salary of a public school teacher
the cost of building a new bridge
a state pension paid to a retired worker
medicines bought for state hospitals
quiz.explanation: A transfer payment moves income from taxpayers to a person without the government receiving any good or service in return, as a pension does. Salaries and medicines are current spending, and a bridge is capital spending.

quiz.question: Capital expenditure by a government is spending on:
options: assets such as roads and hospitals that last for years
wages and running costs used up within the year
benefits paid to households with nothing produced in return
goods bought only from foreign suppliers
quiz.explanation: Capital expenditure buys assets that the state will use for years and that add to the economy's capital stock. Spending used up within the year is current expenditure, and benefits are transfers.

quiz.question: A rising share of people over 65 changing a country's public spending is an example of which reason in the specification?
options: changing age distributions
changing incomes
changing expectations
crowding out
quiz.explanation: The specification gives three reasons for the changing size and pattern of public expenditure. A shift in the share of each age group is a changing age distribution; it raises pension and health spending.

quiz.question: Across countries, as GDP per head rises, public spending as a share of GDP tends to:
options: fall, as households buy their own services
stay at exactly the same share
fall to zero in high-income economies
rise, as demand for health and education grows
quiz.explanation: Demand for health care, education and pensions grows faster than income, and the state provides much of it, so richer economies usually spend a larger share of GDP through the state. A larger tax base also makes that affordable.

quiz.question: An ageing population is most likely to raise public spending on:
options: pensions and health care
primary school places
maternity and child clinics
grants for new university students
quiz.explanation: More people over 65 means more state pensions, which are transfers, and much more health care. Spending on schools and children's services is driven by a young population.

quiz.question: Unemployment benefit paid to a worker who has lost her job is classified as:
options: current expenditure
capital expenditure
an indirect tax
a transfer payment
quiz.explanation: The government receives no good or service in return for the benefit; it moves income to the worker. That makes it a transfer payment rather than current or capital spending on output.

quiz.question: After a pandemic, voters insist that the government keep the wage support it introduced during the emergency. This illustrates:
options: changing expectations
changing age distributions
crowding out
a structural surplus
quiz.explanation: What citizens believe the state should provide has changed: support introduced in a crisis comes to be expected. That is the reason the specification calls changing expectations.

quiz.question: A government spends $20bn on capital projects, $70bn on current spending and $30bn on transfers. GDP is $400bn. Public expenditure as a share of GDP is:
quiz.explanation: Public expenditure includes all three kinds: 20 + 70 + 30 = $120bn, and 120 ÷ 400 × 100 = 30%. Leaving out the transfers gives 22.5%, which understates it.

quiz.question: Crowding out is least likely to occur when:
options: the economy is at full employment
the economy is in a deep recession with idle savings
interest rates are already high and rising
firms are competing hard for scarce loans
quiz.explanation: With spare capacity and savings lying unused, government borrowing need not bid up interest rates or take resources from firms. Near full employment, with high rates and competition for funds, crowding out is greatest.

quiz.question: Crowding out mainly occurs because government borrowing:
options: lowers taxes, so consumption rises
increases exports, so imports fall
reduces the national debt, so rates fall
raises interest rates, so private investment falls
quiz.explanation: The state competes with private borrowers for savers' funds, pushing up interest rates. Projects that were worth doing at the lower rate are postponed, so private investment falls.

quiz.question: Which public spending is most likely to raise long-run productivity?
options: building rail links to industrial zones
paying fuel subsidies to motorists
raising civil service pensions
covering a state bank's losses
quiz.explanation: Transport links to where firms produce cut their costs and add to the economy's capital stock, so output per worker rises. The other items are used up now or keep resources in low-value uses.

quiz.question: Compared with a country whose public spending is 20% of GDP, one whose spending is 50% of GDP will usually need:
options: no taxes on income at all
lower interest rates on its debt
a smaller national debt
a higher share of GDP taken in tax
quiz.explanation: Spending must be paid for. Borrowing can fill a gap for a while, but over time a state that spends half of GDP must raise far more in tax than one that spends a fifth.

quiz.question: A government borrows an extra $50bn to spend, and private investment falls by $15bn as interest rates rise. The share of the extra spending crowded out is:
quiz.explanation: The share crowded out is the fall in private spending over the rise in public spending: 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%. The other 70% is the net addition to total spending.

quiz.question: A worker's marginal rate of income tax rises from 20% to 30%. Of an extra $500 she earns, she now keeps:
quiz.explanation: At a marginal rate of 30% she keeps 70% of the extra $500, which is $350; at 20% she kept $400. The lower reward for extra work is how a tax rise can weaken the incentive to work.

quiz.question: Which of these is an indirect tax?
options: corporation tax on profits
excise duty on cigarettes
income tax on wages
a tax on inherited property
quiz.explanation: An indirect tax is levied on spending and passed on in the price, as a duty on cigarettes is. Taxes on profits, wages and inheritances are levied on income or wealth, so they are direct.

quiz.question: A tax takes 4% of a $10,000 income and 2% of a $50,000 income. The tax is:
options: progressive
proportional
regressive
a direct tax by definition
quiz.explanation: The share of income taken falls as income rises, which is what makes a tax regressive, even though the richer household may pay more in dollars.

quiz.question: According to Laffer curve analysis, cutting a tax rate will raise tax revenue only if:
options: the rate is below the revenue-maximising rate
the tax is an indirect tax
the tax base does not change
the rate is above the revenue-maximising rate
quiz.explanation: Above the peak, a lower rate lets the tax base grow by more than enough to make up for the lower rate. Below the peak, a cut loses revenue because the base grows too little.

quiz.question: Which tax change is most likely to reduce income inequality after tax?
options: raising the tax-free allowance for low earners
raising the standard rate of VAT
cutting the top rate of income tax
replacing income tax with a flat charge per adult
quiz.explanation: Taking the lowest earners out of income tax is a large gain for them as a share of income and a small one for the rich. Higher VAT, a lower top rate and a flat charge all take relatively more from low incomes.

quiz.question: A sales tax is usually regressive because:
options: richer households pay a higher rate on each purchase
lower-income households spend a larger share of their income
it is collected only from firms
it is charged only on luxury goods
quiz.explanation: Everyone pays the same rate on a purchase, but poorer households spend most of what they earn while richer ones save more, so the tax takes a larger share of a low income.

quiz.question: A cut in corporation tax is most likely to attract extra FDI when:
options: the country lacks roads and reliable power
rival locations are similar on skills, markets and stability
every neighbour cuts its rate by the same amount
profits cannot be taken out of the country
quiz.explanation: TNCs choose locations above all for markets, skills and stability. Tax tips the choice between places that are otherwise alike; it cannot make up for missing infrastructure, and a cut that every neighbour matches changes nothing.

quiz.question: A rise in the rate of VAT is best shown on an AD/AS diagram as:
options: a leftward shift of short-run aggregate supply
a rightward shift of aggregate demand
a rightward shift of long-run aggregate supply
no shift of any curve
quiz.explanation: An indirect tax is a cost of production passed on in prices, so SRAS shifts to the left: the price level rises and real output falls.

quiz.question: Income tax is cut by $40bn and the marginal propensity to import is 0.2. Imports rise by about:
options: $32bn
$8bn
$20bn
$2bn
quiz.explanation: Imports rise by the extra disposable income times the share spent on imports: 40 × 0.2 = $8bn. With exports unchanged, the trade balance worsens by that amount.

quiz.question: An income tax cut is most likely to raise real output rather than only the price level when:
options: firms cannot hire any more workers
the economy has plenty of spare capacity
the whole cut is spent on imports
the economy is already at full employment
quiz.explanation: With idle workers and machines, firms meet extra demand by producing more. At full capacity, extra demand mostly raises prices; spending that goes entirely on imports adds nothing to home output.

quiz.question: A project earns $10m a year before tax. If corporation tax is cut from 30% to 20%, the firm's profit after tax rises from:
options: $3m to $2m
$10m to $12m
$7m to $9m
$7m to $8m
quiz.explanation: At 30% the firm keeps 70% of $10m, which is $7m; at 20% it keeps $8m. The higher return after tax is what can draw in foreign direct investment.

quiz.question: Borrowing is most likely to be fair between generations when it pays for:
options: a railway that will carry passengers for decades
a one-off cut in fuel prices
higher pay for current civil servants
a bonus for this year's pensioners
quiz.explanation: Future taxpayers who service and repay the debt also benefit from an asset that lasts. Spending used up now gives today's generation the benefit and leaves a later one the bill.

quiz.question: A government's national debt falls in dollars only when it:
options: reduces the size of its fiscal deficit
runs a smaller cyclical deficit
runs a fiscal surplus
borrows at lower interest rates
quiz.explanation: Any deficit, however small, is borrowed and added to the debt. Only when revenue exceeds spending is there money left to repay debt.

quiz.question: Which of these is an automatic stabiliser?
options: a road-building programme announced in a recession
income tax receipts falling as earnings fall in a recession
a temporary cut in VAT voted through parliament
a one-off grant to households approved by ministers
quiz.explanation: An automatic stabiliser needs no decision: tax receipts fall by themselves when earnings fall. A programme, a vote or an approved grant is discretionary fiscal policy.

quiz.question: The structural deficit is the part of the fiscal deficit that:
options: disappears as the economy recovers from recession
is caused by the automatic stabilisers
would remain even with the economy at full capacity
is owed to lenders in other countries
quiz.explanation: The cyclical part is caused by the downturn and fades with recovery. What would be left at full capacity is structural, and needs a decision on taxes or spending to remove.

quiz.question: A government owes $500bn at the start of the year and runs a fiscal deficit of $30bn. At the end of the year it owes:
options: $30bn
quiz.explanation: The deficit is borrowed and added to the stock of debt: 500 + 30 = $530bn. The deficit is the flow; the debt is the stock it adds to.

quiz.question: A national debt of $300bn carries an average interest rate of 6%. Debt interest each year is about:
options: $50bn
$6bn
$18bn
quiz.explanation: Debt interest is the debt times the average interest rate: 300 × 6 ÷ 100 = $18bn a year, paid from revenue before any other spending.

quiz.question: Which of these would widen a fiscal deficit with no new decision by the government?
options: a recession that cuts tax receipts
a new hospital-building programme
a vote to raise public sector pay
a budget that cuts income tax rates
quiz.explanation: In a recession tax receipts fall and benefit claims rise through the automatic stabilisers, widening the deficit without any policy choice. The other three are decisions.

quiz.question: In response to the global financial crisis of 2008, central banks in the largest economies:
options: raised interest rates to defend their currencies
stopped all purchases of government bonds
cut interest rates close to zero
imposed price controls on housing
quiz.explanation: Aggregate demand was collapsing, so central banks cut their policy rates towards zero and, in several cases, bought government bonds to increase the money supply. Governments added fiscal stimulus.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of a direct control?
options: a rise in the policy interest rate
a cut in the rate of VAT
a new scheme to train welders
a legal limit on the price of bread
quiz.explanation: A direct control sets an outcome by rule instead of working through prices and incentives. An interest rate change is monetary policy, a VAT cut is fiscal and training is supply-side.

quiz.question: A country's inflation is caused by a jump in world oil prices. Raising interest rates to bring it down is likely to:
options: raise both inflation and output
leave output and employment unchanged
cut inflation at the cost of lower output and jobs
shift aggregate supply to the right
quiz.explanation: An oil price jump is a supply shock: prices are already up and output down. Squeezing demand lowers inflation only by reducing output and employment further.

quiz.question: A government cuts public spending to reduce its deficit, but the deficit falls by less than planned. The main reason is that:
options: interest rates on its existing debt fall sharply
the national debt is repaid in full at once
lower output cuts tax receipts and lifts benefit claims
exports collapse as the currency strengthens
quiz.explanation: Spending cuts reduce aggregate demand; as output and incomes fall, the automatic stabilisers reduce tax receipts and raise benefit spending, offsetting part of the saving.

quiz.question: A monthly cash transfer to poor families, paid only if their children attend school, reduces poverty now and also:
options: raises the children's future earning power
raises the price level permanently
reduces the national debt
attracts FDI through lower taxes
quiz.explanation: The condition builds human capital: children who stay in school earn more as adults, which is a supply-side route out of poverty as well as the transfer itself.

quiz.question: A sudden rise in the world prices of food and fuel is best described as:
options: an automatic stabiliser
discretionary fiscal policy
a structural deficit
an external supply shock
quiz.explanation: It starts outside the economy and raises firms' costs, shifting SRAS to the left, so it is an external shock on the supply side.

quiz.question: A central bank raises interest rates on the strength of a growth figure that is later revised down sharply. This illustrates the problem of:
options: risks and uncertainties
inaccurate information
an external shock
crowding out
quiz.explanation: The policy was based on data that turned out to be wrong. Inaccurate information is about the figures themselves; risks and uncertainties are about how a policy will work even when the figures are sound.

quiz.question: Transfer pricing reduces a TNC's total tax bill when:
options: every subsidiary pays the same rate of tax
it sells to independent firms at market prices
profit is shifted into a subsidiary in a low-tax country
it pays its workers more in the high-tax country
quiz.explanation: By setting the internal price so that little profit is recorded where tax is high and more where it is low, the TNC pays less in total. If every country charged the same rate there would be nothing to gain.

quiz.question: The arm's-length principle requires a transfer price to equal:
options: the cost of production in the home country
the price independent firms would agree
the price that minimises total tax
zero for trade within one firm
quiz.explanation: Regulators compare a transfer price with what two unrelated firms would agree in the market, and reassess tax where the internal price was set away from it.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest limit on one government's ability to control a TNC?
options: TNCs are exempt from corporation tax
the TNC can move production and profits abroad
TNCs are not allowed to trade across borders
TNCs must publish every internal price
quiz.explanation: Mobility is the core limit: a government that taxes or regulates harshly risks losing the investment and jobs to another country, so acting alone it can go only so far.

quiz.question: Tax avoidance differs from tax evasion because avoidance:
options: is illegal, while evasion is not
is legal, while evasion is not
applies only to indirect taxes
is carried out only by individuals
quiz.explanation: Avoidance arranges affairs within the law to pay less tax; evasion is illegal non-payment. That is why TNC avoidance is fought with new rules and agreements rather than prosecution.

quiz.question: When US interest rates rise sharply, the most likely effect on the global economy is that:
options: emerging economies can borrow more cheaply
world trade stops for a year
emerging-economy currencies weaken as capital flows out
every exchange rate stays unchanged
quiz.explanation: Higher US returns draw capital out of emerging economies, so their currencies fall and their own borrowing costs rise: a policy change in one large economy with a global impact.

practice.question: Define the term 'transfer payments'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate points. Say who pays whom, and then what makes this kind of spending different from paying a teacher or building a road.
Payments made by the government to individuals, such as pensions, unemployment benefits or child grants (1 mark), for which no good or service is received in return, so they redistribute income rather than buy output (1 mark). An example alone, without the "nothing in return" point, earns only the first mark.

practice.question: Explain how an increase in government borrowing to finance public expenditure may lead to crowding out. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants linked stages for an Explain. Start from what the government does to raise the money, and follow it to what happens to private spending — each stage should cause the next.
Knowledge: crowding out is a fall in private sector spending caused by a rise in public spending (1 mark). The government sells bonds and competes with private borrowers for savers' funds (1 mark). This pushes up interest rates across the economy (1 mark). At higher interest rates some private investment and borrowed consumption is no longer worthwhile, so the rise in total spending is smaller than the rise in public spending (1 mark).

practice.question: A country's income tax charges nothing on the first $5,000 of income, 10% on income between $5,000 and $25,000, and 30% on income above $25,000. Calculate the average rate of income tax paid by a person earning $40,000. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for the working as well as the answer (Appendix 6). Work band by band from the bottom, add up the tax, and only then turn it into a share of the whole income — the average rate is not the rate on the top slice.
Tax = 0 + 10% × $20,000 + 30% × $15,000 = $2,000 + $4,500 = $6,500 (1 mark). Average rate = $6,500 ÷ $40,000 × 100 = 16.25% (1 mark). Giving 30%, the marginal rate, earns no marks.

practice.question: A country's income tax charges nothing on the first $5,000 of income, 10% on income between $5,000 and $25,000, and 30% on income above $25,000. Calculate the average rate of income tax paid at incomes of $20,000 and $80,000, and use your answers to state whether the tax is progressive. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for workings (Appendix 6). Do each income separately, band by band, before comparing, and remember that the test of a tax structure is the share of income taken, not the dollars paid.
At $20,000: tax = 10% × $15,000 = $1,500 (1 mark); average rate = $1,500 ÷ $20,000 = 7.5% (1 mark). At $80,000: tax = $2,000 + 30% × $55,000 = $2,000 + $16,500 = $18,500; average rate = $18,500 ÷ $80,000 ≈ 23.1% (1 mark). The average rate rises as income rises, so the tax is progressive (1 mark).

practice.question: Analyse how an increase in the rate of an indirect tax may affect the price level and real output in an economy. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants depth for an Analyse: one route followed through several linked stages. Decide first which curve moves, and why, before you describe what happens to prices and output.
Knowledge: an indirect tax is a tax on spending, such as VAT or an excise duty (1 mark). Application: firms pass the higher tax on to buyers, raising their costs of supplying goods (1 mark). Analysis, first stage: short-run aggregate supply shifts to the left (1 mark). Analysis, second stage: the price level rises, a one-off rise of the cost-push kind (1 mark). Analysis, third stage: real output falls along the aggregate demand curve, so firms need fewer workers (1 mark). Development: the rise in prices continues only if workers win higher wages to compensate, setting off a wage-price spiral (1 mark).

practice.question: Evaluate the likely economic effects of a significant cut in the rates of direct taxation. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. Plan the effects on each of the specification's headings before writing — incentives, revenue, distribution, output and employment, prices, the trade balance and FDI — and decide in advance what your judgement will depend on.
Level 1 lists effects with little explanation. Level 2 explains one or two chains, such as a cut in income tax raising disposable income, consumption and aggregate demand. Level 3 develops several chains with application: higher output and employment where there is spare capacity; stronger incentives to work and invest; a lower corporation tax drawing in FDI; but also more imports worsening the trade balance, demand-pull pressure near full capacity, lost revenue unless rates were above the Laffer peak, and a wider gap between post-tax incomes if the top rate is cut. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement that follows from the argument: the effects depend on how much spare capacity there is, which taxes are cut and for whom, where the rates sit relative to the revenue-maximising rate, and how the lost revenue is replaced — by borrowing, spending cuts or other taxes.

practice.question: Examine the significance of a large national debt for an economy. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants a chain of reasoning and a brief assessment for an Examine, so save room for a judgement. Use the specification's three headings to organise the chains, and decide what makes a debt more or less of a problem.
Level 1 states that a large debt is bad, with little explanation. Level 2 explains one chain: a large debt must be serviced, so interest takes revenue that could fund schools or tax cuts. Level 3 develops two or three chains with application — interest payments as a share of revenue; heavy borrowing pushing up interest rates and crowding out private investment; future taxpayers repaying debt for spending they did not benefit from. The brief assessment that lifts an answer to the top of the range weighs its significance: it depends on the interest rate relative to growth, whether the debt is owed at home or abroad and in which currency, and whether it paid for assets that last.

practice.question: Discuss the effectiveness of the demand-side policies used in response to the global financial crisis of 2008. (14 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and a critical assessment. Separate the fiscal response from the monetary response before writing, and decide how you will judge effectiveness — against what would have happened without them, and against their later costs.
Level 1 describes the crisis with little explanation of policy. Level 2 explains one response: stimulus spending and tax cuts raised aggregate demand, or near-zero interest rates cut the cost of borrowing. Level 3 develops both with application: fiscal stimulus in the US and China replaced collapsing private demand; interest rate cuts and bond buying to increase the money supply supported spending and asset prices; coordination through the G20 limited leakage into imports. Against that, banks were unwilling to lend, so low rates reached firms slowly; national debts rose sharply; and very low rates for years raised asset prices and wealth inequality. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: the policies were effective in preventing a depression, less effective in producing a fast recovery, and left costs in debt that shaped policy for a decade.

practice.question: Evaluate the policies a government might use to reduce a large fiscal deficit. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. Plan the tools before writing — fiscal, monetary, supply-side, exchange-rate policy and direct controls — and decide what the judgement will turn on, such as how much spare capacity there is and whether the deficit is structural or cyclical.
Level 1 lists policies with little explanation. Level 2 explains how one or two work: higher taxes and lower spending close the gap directly; growth raises revenue. Level 3 develops several with chains and application: fiscal tightening reduces aggregate demand, so output and tax receipts fall and the deficit falls by less than planned; low interest rates cut the cost of servicing the debt; supply-side reform raises trend growth but takes years; a lower currency helps exports but raises the burden of foreign-currency debt; pay freezes are quick but can damage services. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: a cyclical deficit needs growth rather than cuts, a structural deficit needs a decision; cutting current spending and subsidies harms growth less than cutting capital spending; and gradual consolidation with supportive monetary policy is usually more effective than sharp cuts in a weak economy.

practice.question: Evaluate the measures governments can use to control the activities of transnational corporations (TNCs). (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. The specification pairs the measures with the limits on them, so plan both before writing, and decide whether acting alone or acting together is the key to your judgement.
Level 1 describes TNCs with little explanation of measures. Level 2 explains one or two measures: regulating transfer prices so they match arm's-length market prices; a minimum tax on profits. Level 3 develops the measures and their limits with application: transfer pricing rules protect the tax base, but brands and patents have no market price to check against; country-by-country reporting exposes profits booked where there is little activity; a global minimum tax removes much of the gain from tax havens; but TNCs are mobile, well advised and able to lobby, and a small tax authority may lack the staff and information to audit them. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: measures by one country alone are limited by mobility, so their effectiveness depends on international cooperation, and on developing countries having the capacity to enforce what is agreed.

flashcards.front: What is capital expenditure?
flashcards.back: Public spending on assets that last for years: roads, schools, hospitals, ports. It adds to the economy's capital stock.

flashcards.front: What is current expenditure?
flashcards.back: Public spending on goods and services used up within the year: the salaries of teachers and nurses, medicines, running costs.

flashcards.front: What is a transfer payment?
flashcards.back: A payment from government to an individual with no good or service received in return, such as a pension or unemployment benefit.

flashcards.front: Name the three reasons the specification gives for changes in the size and pattern of public spending.
flashcards.back: Changing incomes, changing age distributions and changing expectations.

flashcards.front: How does an ageing population change public spending?
flashcards.back: It raises spending on pensions and health care, may reduce spending on schools, and narrows the base of workers paying tax.

flashcards.front: How can public spending raise productivity and growth?
flashcards.back: Spending on infrastructure, education and health raises output per worker and shifts long-run aggregate supply to the right.

flashcards.front: What is crowding out?
flashcards.back: A fall in private sector spending caused by a rise in public spending, mainly because government borrowing pushes up interest rates.

flashcards.front: When is crowding out most and least likely?
flashcards.back: Most likely near full employment with high interest rates; least likely in a deep recession with spare capacity and idle savings.

flashcards.front: Why does a large state mean high taxes?
flashcards.back: Spending must be paid for. Borrowing can fill a gap for a time, but the debt and its interest are paid from future taxes.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a direct and an indirect tax?
flashcards.back: A direct tax is levied on income or wealth (income tax, corporation tax); an indirect tax is levied on spending and passed on in the price (VAT, excise duties).

flashcards.front: Define a progressive tax.
flashcards.back: A tax that takes a rising share of income as income rises.

flashcards.front: Define a proportional tax.
flashcards.back: A tax that takes the same share of income at every level of income.

flashcards.front: Define a regressive tax.
flashcards.back: A tax that takes a falling share of income as income rises, even if richer people pay more in dollars.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the marginal and the average rate of tax?
flashcards.back: The marginal rate is the tax on the last dollar earned; the average rate is total tax divided by total income.

flashcards.front: How can a rise in income tax affect incentives to work?
flashcards.back: It lowers the reward for extra work, so some work less or move abroad; people with an income target may work more.

flashcards.front: What does the Laffer curve show?
flashcards.back: Tax revenue rises with the tax rate up to a peak and then falls, as very high rates shrink the tax base.

flashcards.front: When does cutting a tax rate raise revenue on Laffer analysis?
flashcards.back: Only when the rate is above the revenue-maximising rate — and nobody knows exactly where that is.

flashcards.front: How does raising VAT affect income distribution?
flashcards.back: It takes a larger share of low incomes, because poorer households spend more of what they earn, so it widens inequality.

flashcards.front: How does a cut in income tax affect real output and employment?
flashcards.back: Disposable income and consumption rise, AD shifts right, and with spare capacity firms produce more and hire more workers.

flashcards.front: How does a rise in indirect taxes affect the price level?
flashcards.back: It raises costs passed on in prices, shifting SRAS left: a one-off rise in the price level and lower real output.

flashcards.front: How does a cut in income tax affect the trade balance?
flashcards.back: Part of the extra disposable income is spent on imports, so imports rise and the trade balance tends to worsen.

flashcards.front: How can a cut in corporation tax affect FDI flows?
flashcards.back: It raises the post-tax return on investing in the country, attracting inward FDI, though markets, skills and stability usually matter more.

flashcards.front: What is a fiscal deficit?
flashcards.back: The amount by which public expenditure exceeds government revenue in one year; it is borrowed.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a fiscal deficit and the national debt?
flashcards.back: A deficit is a flow over one year; the national debt is the stock of past borrowing still owed. Each deficit adds to the debt.

flashcards.front: What is an automatic stabiliser?
flashcards.back: A change in tax receipts or benefit spending that happens without any decision as the economy changes, dampening the cycle.

flashcards.front: What is discretionary fiscal policy?
flashcards.back: A deliberate decision to change tax rates or public spending, such as a stimulus package.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a structural and a cyclical deficit?
flashcards.back: The cyclical deficit is caused by the economic cycle and fades in recovery; the structural deficit would remain at full capacity.

flashcards.front: Name four factors that influence the size of a fiscal deficit.
flashcards.back: The economic cycle, spending and tax decisions, interest rates on the debt, and shocks such as disasters or banking crises.

flashcards.front: What is debt servicing?
flashcards.back: Paying the interest on the national debt and repaying or refinancing it as it falls due.

flashcards.front: What does intergenerational equity mean for public debt?
flashcards.back: Fairness between generations: future taxpayers repay today's borrowing, which is fairer when it paid for assets that benefit them too.

flashcards.front: Name the five policy tools in 4.3.5.
flashcards.back: Fiscal policy, monetary policy, exchange-rate policy, supply-side policies and direct controls.

flashcards.front: What are direct controls?
flashcards.back: Rules that set outcomes directly: price caps, wage controls, limits on imports or exports, and controls on capital flows.

flashcards.front: How did governments respond to the global financial crisis of 2008?
flashcards.back: Fiscal stimulus and tax cuts, interest rates cut close to zero, and central banks buying bonds to increase the money supply.

flashcards.front: What is transfer pricing?
flashcards.back: The price one part of a TNC charges another; set away from the market price, it moves profit to low-tax countries.

flashcards.front: What is the arm's-length principle?
flashcards.back: A transfer price must equal the price two independent firms would agree in the market.

flashcards.front: Give three limits to a government's ability to control TNCs.
flashcards.back: TNCs can move production and profit abroad; governments lack information on internal prices; one country cannot tax beyond its borders.

flashcards.front: Name the three problems facing policymakers in the specification.
flashcards.back: Inaccurate information, risks and uncertainties, and inability to control external shocks.

mistakes.title: Confusing the fiscal deficit with the national debt
mistakes.looks_like: "The government cut the deficit, so the national debt fell."
mistakes.why: The deficit is a yearly flow of new borrowing and the debt is the stock it adds to. A smaller deficit still adds to the debt, only more slowly.
mistakes.instead: Say that the debt falls in dollars only in a surplus year, and that the debt ratio can fall if GDP grows faster than the debt.

mistakes.title: Calling a sales tax proportional
mistakes.looks_like: "VAT is proportional because everyone pays the same rate."
mistakes.why: Tax structures are judged by the share of income taken. Poorer households spend a larger share of their income, so a sales tax takes a larger share of it.
mistakes.instead: Compare the tax with income at two or more income levels, and call it regressive when the share falls as income rises.

mistakes.title: Treating crowding out as certain and complete
mistakes.looks_like: "Government spending has no effect because it all crowds out private investment."
mistakes.why: Crowding out is usually partial, and close to zero in a deep recession when savings are idle and interest rates are low.
mistakes.instead: State the conditions: crowding out is larger near full capacity with high rates and smaller with spare capacity.

mistakes.title: Calling a stimulus package an automatic stabiliser
mistakes.looks_like: "The government's new spending programme was an automatic stabiliser."
mistakes.why: Automatic stabilisers are changes that happen without a decision, such as falling tax receipts in a recession. A programme someone decided on is discretionary.
mistakes.instead: Ask whether anyone had to decide it. If yes, it is discretionary fiscal policy.

mistakes.title: Claiming the Laffer curve proves tax cuts pay for themselves
mistakes.looks_like: "Cutting the tax rate will raise revenue because of the Laffer curve."
mistakes.why: A cut raises revenue only above the revenue-maximising rate, and nobody knows where that rate is. Below it, a cut loses revenue.
mistakes.instead: Say where the economy is likely to be relative to the peak, and how uncertain that is.

mistakes.title: Drawing an indirect tax rise as an AD shift
mistakes.looks_like: "Higher VAT reduces demand, so AD shifts left and prices fall."
mistakes.why: An indirect tax is added to firms' costs and prices, so short-run aggregate supply shifts left and the price level rises.
mistakes.instead: Shift SRAS left for an indirect tax rise; shift AD for a change in income tax.

mistakes.title: Calling TNC tax avoidance illegal
mistakes.looks_like: "TNCs break the law by using transfer pricing to avoid tax."
mistakes.why: Tax avoidance is legal; evasion is not. Transfer pricing becomes a problem when the price is set away from the market price, which regulation then challenges.
mistakes.instead: Distinguish avoidance from evasion, and name the measure that closes the route: arm's-length rules, reporting or a minimum tax.

diagrams.title: Public Expenditure: Three Kinds
diagrams.description: IAL 4.3.5 · 1a: one economy's public expenditure split into capital expenditure, current expenditure and transfer payments, in dollars and as a share of GDP.
checklist: Capital expenditure: assets that last, such as roads and hospitals
Current expenditure: salaries, medicines and running costs used up within the year
Transfer payments: pensions and benefits, with nothing produced in return

chains.title: Crowding out, in figures
steps: The government sells bonds to borrow $20bn for new public spending.
Competing for savers' funds, it pushes interest rates up from 4% to 5%.
At the higher rate, firms postpone $8bn of investment projects.
Total spending rises by $12bn, not $20bn: 40% has been crowded out.
chains.result: Crowding out makes public spending less powerful than it looks, but rarely powerless. It is largest near full capacity with high interest rates and smallest in a deep recession.

chains.title: Automatic stabilisers in a recession
steps: Output falls; workers lose overtime and jobs, and profits shrink.
With no decision taken, income tax, corporation tax and VAT receipts fall by $8bn and, at the same time, claims for unemployment support rise by $4bn.
Disposable income falls by less than earnings, so spending is cushioned.
The deficit widens by $12bn: this is the cyclical deficit, and it shrinks again in recovery.
chains.result: The stabilisers act at once and need no legislation, which is their advantage over discretionary policy. They are strongest where taxes are progressive and benefits generous.

chains.title: Transfer pricing, in figures
steps: A TNC mines copper in Country H at a cost of $60m and sells it to its own trading arm in Country L for $65m, below the world price of $100m.
Only $5m of profit is recorded in H, taxed at 30%: $1.5m.
The trading arm resells at the world price and records $35m of profit in L, taxed at 5%: $1.75m.
At the arm's-length price H would have taxed all $40m of profit and collected $12m; it collects $10.5m less.
chains.result: The copper, the mine and the workers are all in Country H; the profit is not. That is why transfer prices are regulated against the arm's-length market price.

chains.title: The global financial crisis of 2008 and the response
steps: Losses on US housing loans spread to banks worldwide.
Banks stop lending; spending, trade and output fall across the world.
Governments pass stimulus packages; central banks slash rates to near zero and buy government bonds.
Output stabilises and national debts rise sharply.
chains.result: Demand-side policy on this scale prevented a depression. Its costs — higher debt and years of very low interest rates — shaped fiscal and monetary policy for the following decade.

evaluation.title: Tax rises or spending cuts to close a deficit?
evaluation.content: Neither is painless, and the answer depends on the economy and the deficit. **Ask first whether the deficit is structural or cyclical.** A cyclical deficit closes with recovery and needs no cuts; a structural one needs a decision. Tax rises spread the burden but may weaken incentives; spending cuts shrink the state but fall on the users of public services, and cuts to capital spending harm future growth. In a weak economy either reduces demand, so output and tax receipts fall and the deficit shrinks by less than planned.

evaluation.title: Is a large national debt a problem?
evaluation.content: The size alone says little. **What matters is the cost of servicing it and the capacity to carry it.** A debt at low interest rates in a growing economy, owed in the home currency to domestic savers, can be carried for decades, as Japan shows. The same ratio owed in foreign currency, at rising rates, in a slow-growing economy, can force painful cuts. And debt that paid for lasting assets leaves future generations something to show for it.

evaluation.title: Can governments control TNCs?
evaluation.content: Acting alone, only partly. **TNCs are mobile, well advised and better informed about their own affairs than any tax authority.** Transfer pricing rules work best for commodities with a world price and least for brands and patents. International agreements — the OECD minimum tax, shared reporting — change the balance, because they remove the option of moving profit to a country with no tax. Their effectiveness depends on enough countries joining and on developing countries having the capacity to enforce them.
